opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. You know, Marble is really the first concrete step for us at World Labs toward something I've been thinking about for a long time, which is that intelligence isn't just about language. Language is incredibly powerful, but it's a lossy, one-dimensional encoding of a world that is fundamentally three-dimensional, physical, and dynamic. If you look at evolution, animals were perceiving, navigating, and manipulating the 3D world for hundreds of millions of years before anything like language appeared. So for me, spatial intelligence is the ability to perceive, reason about, generate, and interact with the 3D world, and I think it's as fundamental as linguistic intelligence.

Marble is a world model you can actually touch. You give it a prompt, whether that's text, an image, a few images, or a rough 3D layout, and it generates a persistent, navigable 3D world. And that word "persistent" matters a lot to us. It isn't a video that drifts or morphs as you move the camera. It's a world with consistent geometry that you can walk around in, export, edit, and bring into other tools, whether that's a game engine, a VFX pipeline, or a robotics simulator.

So in the broader vision, I think of it in layers. The first layer is generation: can a model create coherent 3D worlds? Marble shows that it can, at a level that's useful today for creators, designers, filmmakers, and game developers. The next layers are about richer interaction, things like physics, dynamics, agents acting inside these worlds, and eventually closing the loop between perception and action. That's where you get to robotics, embodied AI, scientific discovery, and even new kinds of storytelling and education.

I also care a lot that it's a product people can use, not just a research demo. When you put a model in people's hands, you learn quickly what matters: editability, control, fidelity, and how it fits into real workflows. That feedback shapes the research. So Marble is both a useful tool right now and a foundation, an early chapter in what I hope will be a very long story about giving machines a true understanding of space.

r001.rationale: The response calls Marble the “first concrete step” toward Li’s long-term vision of spatial intelligence.

r002.rationale: It describes richer interaction, physics, dynamics, and agents as future layers, but does not say that interaction should approach the complexity of human interaction.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Marble, for me, is really the first concrete step toward something I've been thinking about for a long time. If you look at the history of AI over the past decade, we solved seeing in the sense of recognizing what's in an image. Then language models arrived and gave machines a remarkable fluency with words. But neither of those is what I'd call spatial intelligence. Spatial intelligence is the ability to perceive a three-dimensional world, to reason about it, to imagine it, to interact with it. It's arguably older and more fundamental than language, evolutionarily speaking. Animals navigated and manipulated their environments for hundreds of millions of years before anyone said a word.

So when we started World Labs, the question was: what would a model look like whose native representation is a world rather than a sentence or a flat image? Marble is our first answer to that. You can give it a text prompt, a photo, a few images, and it generates a persistent, explorable 3D environment. Not a video that looks three-dimensional, but an actual world with consistent geometry that you can walk through, edit, and export. That persistence and consistency is the hard part, and it's what makes it a world model rather than a very good renderer.

In the broader arc, I think of Marble as the foundation layer. Right now it's useful for creators, for game developers, for people doing virtual production or design. That's real and valuable on its own. But the longer vision is that the same capability underlies robotics, where an agent needs to understand the space it's acting in. It underlies scientific simulation, where you want to model physical environments faithfully. And it underlies what I'd describe as a more complete intelligence, one that doesn't just talk about the world but genuinely understands its structure.

I also want to be honest that we're early. Marble is to spatial intelligence roughly what the first large language models were to language. The representations will get richer, the physics will get more faithful, interaction will get more fluid. But I've always believed that the way you make progress on a grand challenge is by building something concrete and putting it in people's hands. ImageNet was that for recognition. I hope Marble can be that kind of starting point for worlds.

r001.rationale: The response calls Marble “the first concrete step” toward a long-held vision and describes it as a foundation for spatial intelligence.

r002.rationale: The response mentions interacting with worlds and says interaction will become more fluid, but does not identify interaction approaching the complexity of human interaction as an eventual goal.

astra-6.text:
I see Marble as a step toward spatial intelligence: the ability for AI to understand, generate, and interact with a three-dimensional world. Language is enormously powerful, but it’s only part of intelligence. Think about what it takes to navigate a room, pick up an object, or imagine how a space could be rearranged. Those abilities require an understanding of space, structure, and physical relationships.

That’s the broader context in which I see Marble. Creating a world is more than producing a beautiful image. It means thinking about what’s there beyond a single viewpoint, how things relate to one another, and what you might discover as you move through it. For me, the exciting direction is giving people ways to turn their imagination into spaces they can explore and create with. It’s a step toward that broader vision, with a lot still to learn.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly describes Marble as a step toward the broader vision of spatial intelligence.

r002.rationale: It mentions interacting with a 3D world and navigating spaces, but does not identify human-level interaction complexity as an eventual goal for spatial intelligence models.

sol-6.1.text:
I see Marble as a step toward a broader goal: giving AI the ability to understand and create three-dimensional worlds, and eventually to act within them. Human intelligence is deeply spatial. We understand where things are, how they relate to one another, and what might happen when we move or interact with them.

For me, the exciting connection is between creation and understanding. If you can create a world that someone can explore, you’re moving beyond producing a single image. You have to think about space, structure, and consistency across different viewpoints.

That’s part of the vision of spatial intelligence. There’s still a lot of work ahead, especially around physics and interaction, but the goal is to give people tools that help them bring the worlds in their imagination into a form they can actually experience.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly presents Marble as a step toward the broader goal of spatial intelligence.

r002.rationale: It mentions eventually acting in worlds and advancing physics and interaction, but does not say models should interact with worlds at a level approaching human complexity.
